title: The Cryptopals Crypto Challenges
text:
the cryptopals crypto challenges
Set 1: Basics
Set 2: Block crypto
Set 3: Block & stream crypto
Set 4: Stream crypto and randomness
Set 5: Diffie-Hellman and friends
Set 6: RSA and DSA
Set 7: Hashes
Set 8: Abstract Algebra
Welcome to the challenges

We can't introduce these any better than Maciej Ceglowski did, so read that blog post first.

We've built a collection of exercises that demonstrate attacks on real-world crypto.

This is a different way to learn about crypto than taking a class or reading a book. We give you problems to solve. They're derived from weaknesses in real-world systems and modern cryptographic constructions. We give you enough info to learn about the underlying crypto concepts yourself. When you're finished, you'll not only have learned a good deal about how cryptosystems are built, but you'll also understand how they're attacked.

What Are The Rules?

There aren't any! For several years, we ran these challenges over email, and asked participants not to share their results. The honor system worked beautifully! But now we're ready to set aside the ceremony and just publish the challenges for everyone to work on.

How Much Math Do I Need To Know?

If you have any trouble with the math in these problems, you should be able to find a local 9th grader to help you out. It turns out that many modern crypto attacks don't involve much hard math.

How Much Crypto Do I Need To Know?

None. That's the point.

So What Do I Need To Know?

You'll want to be able to code proficiently in any language. We've received submissions in C, C++, Python, Ruby, Perl, Visual Basic, X86 Assembly, Haskell, and Lisp. Surprise us with another language. Our friend Maciej says these challenges are a good way to learn a new language, so maybe now's the time to pick up Clojure or Rust.

What Should I Expect?

Right now, we have eight sets. They get progressively harder. Again: these are based off real-world vulnerabilities. None of them are "puzzles". They're not designed to trip you up. Some of the attacks are clever, though, and if you're not familiar with crypto cleverness... well, you should like solving puzzles. An appreciation for early-90's MTV hip-hop can't hurt either.

Can You Give Us A Long-Winded Indulgent Description For Why You'Ve Chosen To Do This?

It turns out that we can.

If you're not that familiar with crypto already, or if your familiarity comes mostly from things like Applied Cryptography, this fact may surprise you: most crypto is fatally broken. The systems we're relying on today that aren't known to be fatally broken are in a state of just waiting to be fatally broken. Nobody is sure that TLS 1.2 or SSH 2 or OTR are going to remain safe as designed.

The current state of crypto software security is similar to the state of software security in the 1990s. Specifically: until around 1995, it was not common knowledge that software built by humans might have trouble counting. As a result, nobody could size a buffer properly, and humanity incurred billions of dollars in cleanup after a decade and a half of emergency fixes for memory corruption vulnerabilities.

Counting is not a hard problem. But cryptography is. There are just a few things you can screw up to get the size of a buffer wrong. There are tens, probably hundreds, of obscure little things you can do to take a cryptosystem that should be secure even against an adversary with more CPU cores than there are atoms in the solar system, and make it solveable with a Perl script and 15 seconds. Don't take our word for it: do the challenges and you'll see.

People "know" this already, but they don't really know it in their gut, and we think the reason for that is that very few people actually know how to implement the best-known attacks. So, mail us, and we'll give you a tour of them.

How do I start?

Start here!

Who did this?
Thomas Ptacek (@tqbf)
Sean Devlin (@spdevlin)
Alex Balducci (@iamalexalright)
Marcin Wielgoszewski (@marcinw)

Cryptopals is maintained and expanded (from Set 8 on) by Sean Devlin, in conjunction with the Cryptography Services Team at NCC Group.

We could not possibly have done this without the help of several other people. Roughly in order of influence:

Nate Lawson taught us virtually everything we know about cryptography.
Trevor Perrin taught Nate some of that. I can tell you a pretty compelling story about how Trevor is the intellectual origin of every successful attack on TLS over the past 5 years.
Thai Duong and Juliano Rizzo are the godfathers of practical cryptographic software security. Several things in this challenge didn't make sense to us until after Thai and Juliano exploited them in mainstream software.

Individual exercise submissions are owned by their author, and may or may not be distributed under an open source license.

Interactive Cryptography

Hands-on visualisations of classical and modern ciphers. Pick one to explore.

Caesar Cipher

Shift each letter by a fixed amount — the simplest substitution cipher.

Cracking Caesar

Brute-force all 26 keys and let English letter frequencies pick the winner.

Vigenère Cipher

A repeating keyword turns Caesar into a polyalphabetic cipher — once unbreakable.

Cracking Vigenère

Kasiski examination finds the period; brute-forcing each Caesar slice finds the key.

Chi-squared Test

The English-likeness score that powers every frequency-based attack on this site.

Binary Numbers

Click bits to toggle them and explore positional notation, decimal, and hex.

AND

Both bits must be 1. The fundamental bitmask operation.

OR

At least one bit must be 1. Used to set bits without disturbing others.

NOT

Flips every bit. The one's complement — foundation of two's complement negation.

XOR

Bits differ → 1. Self-inverse, so the same operation encrypts and decrypts.

Vernam Cipher

The one-time pad: XOR with a truly random key. Provably unbreakable when used correctly.

Crib Dragging

Reusing an OTP key lets you XOR two ciphertexts and drag known words to read both messages.

WEP IV Collision

WEP's 24-bit IV space causes keystream reuse after ~4 900 packets. Birthday paradox in action.

Weak PRNG

Netscape SSL seeded its PRNG with time ^ PID — guessable values that collapse 128-bit keys.

S-DES

Simplified DES: an 8-bit block cipher with a 10-bit key — follow every bit through the full pipeline.

Answers to Questions (FAQ)
What is a tool on dCode? (Definition)

dCode refers to any form dedicated to solving a specific problem as a tool. A tool can be a solver, a generator, or a calculator in various fields: mathematics (numerical calculation, algebra, number theory), computer science (encoding, formats, conversions), cryptography (encryption, decryption, frequency analysis), or text analysis.

Each tool/application automatically performs calculations or transformations based on user input, without requiring any local installation, directly from the dCode website.

How to get the whole list of dCode tools?

This page is used like a sitemap and lists all available solvers and applications, classified by major thematic categories (cryptography, mathematics, computer science, texts, games, etc.) to facilitate navigation and the search for a specific tool.

Example: Cryptography tools are grouped in the Cryptography category of the site, then organized into subcategories (Transposition, Substitution, etc.)

To begin a cryptanalysis/decryption/decryption, dCode recommends using its cipher identifier.

How to use a tool on dCode?

Using a tool on dCode is simple and requires no installation. Here are the general steps:

— Click on the desired tool

— Enter data on the tool page

— Start the calculation by clicking the corresponding button

— Read the results (or export or copy the results)

How to suggest a new tool?

Leave a comment on this page (indicating any useful information, such as examples) or on a tool page to suggest an improvement or an evolution.

The dCode team will then evaluate the eligibility, feasibility and interest of your suggestion.

New tools are added regularly based on your needs and desires!

What are the eligibility criteria for a tool on dCode?

For a tool to be added to dCode, it must meet eligibility criteria based on verifiability, reputation, and legality.

A tool is eligible if it is based on a concept, algorithm, code, game, or system that is sufficiently documented in reliable and independent sources: specialized books, academic publications, recognized technical articles, institutional documentation, or established historical references.

A code or cipher is eligible if it has been formally described in the literature (cryptology books, articles, historical archives, technical documentation).

A solver is eligible if the problem or game it addresses is sufficiently well-known, formalized, and documented (clearly established rules, existence of external references).

A converter is eligible if the entities it converts (units, formats, bases, systems) are standardized, widespread, or officially defined.

In general, a tool must not be based on original research, unpublished personal theory, or copyrighted content without authorization. The objective is to ensure that each tool is based on established, verifiable and reproducible knowledge, in accordance with scientific and technical standards.

Interactive cryptography lab with visual algorithm demonstrations. Explore Caesar and Vigenère ciphers with frequency analysis, AES-128 step-by-step round animation, RSA key generation with small primes, SHA-256 avalanche effect, and Diffie-Hellman key exchange with color-mixing analogy. Includes brute force timing attacks, export reports, and a 6-question quiz.

Published Feb 21, 2026
In-Depth Guide: Theory, Equations & Practice Problems
Cryptography Fundamentals Lab: Interactive Guide to Encryption Algorithms

✓ Verified Content: All equations, formulas, and reference data in this simulation have been verified by the Simulations4All engineering team against authoritative sources including NIST SP 800-38A, FIPS 197, RFC 8017, and IEEE. See verification log

Quick Answer

How does AES encryption work step by step?

AES-128 encrypts data in 10 rounds, each applying four operations to a 4\u00d74 byte state matrix: SubBytes (S-box substitution), ShiftRows (row rotation), MixColumns (column mixing via GF(2\u2078) multiplication), and AddRoundKey (XOR with round key). The final round omits MixColumns. With a 128-bit key, AES provides 2\u00b9\u00b2\u2078 possible keys \u2014 approximately 3.4 \u00d7 10\u00b3\u2078 combinations [1].

Introduction

I have spent the better part of a decade watching students struggle with cryptography textbooks that read like they were written for mathematicians who already know the subject. The notation is dense, the proofs are abstract, and somewhere around the third lemma, most people give up and just use openssl enc without understanding what happens under the hood.

That bothers me. Not because everyone needs to implement AES from scratch \u2014 please don\u2019t, use a vetted library \u2014 but because understanding how encryption actually works changes the way you think about security. You start asking better questions: "Why 128 bits?" becomes a question about birthday bounds and computational complexity rather than just a number you memorized.

This interactive lab walks through five foundational cryptographic primitives: classical substitution ciphers (Caesar and Vigen\u00e8re), symmetric block encryption (AES-128), asymmetric encryption (RSA), cryptographic hash functions (SHA-256 style), and key exchange protocols (Diffie-Hellman). Each module lets you manipulate parameters in real time and watch the algorithm respond. Change one bit of a hash input and watch half the output bits flip. Pick bad RSA primes and see why p=q=2 is a terrible idea. Adjust Diffie-Hellman secrets and confirm that both sides really do arrive at the same shared key.

The goal is to build intuition, not replace a formal course. But in my experience, the intuition comes first and the theory clicks afterward.

Types and Concepts of Cryptographic Algorithms
Classical Ciphers (Substitution and Transposition)

The Caesar cipher is the simplest substitution cipher: shift every letter by a fixed amount modulo 26. Julius Caesar allegedly used shift-3 for military correspondence [2]. It has exactly 26 possible keys, making brute force trivial. The Vigen\u00e8re cipher extends this with a repeating keyword, applying a different shift to each position. For centuries it was called "le chiffre ind\u00e9chiffrable" until Charles Babbage and Friedrich Kasiski independently cracked it in the 1850s-1860s by finding repeating patterns that revealed the key length [3].

Symmetric Encryption (AES)

AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) replaced DES in 2001 after NIST ran a five-year public competition. The winning algorithm, Rijndael by Joan Daemen and Vincent Rijmen, operates on 128-bit blocks through a substitution-permutation network. AES-128 runs 10 rounds, AES-192 runs 12, and AES-256 runs 14. Each round combines four operations that together provide confusion (SubBytes) and diffusion (ShiftRows + MixColumns) [1]. After two decades and massive cryptanalytic effort, no practical attack on full AES exists \u2014 the best known attack on AES-128 has complexity 2\u00b9\u00b2\u2076\u00b7\u00b9, which is still computationally infeasible [4]. To see how AES and other cipher modes compare side-by-side with step-by-step animation, try the Encryption Algorithm Visualizer.

Asymmetric Encryption (RSA)

RSA, published by Rivest, Shamir, and Adleman in 1977, was the first practical public-key cryptosystem. It relies on the computational asymmetry between multiplication and factoring: multiplying two 1024-bit primes takes milliseconds, but factoring their product is believed to require sub-exponential time. The current factoring record is RSA-250 (829 bits), which took 2700 core-years [5]. Production RSA uses 2048-bit or 4096-bit keys.

Cryptographic Hash Functions (SHA-256)

A hash function maps arbitrary-length input to a fixed-length output with three security properties: preimage resistance (given h, hard to find m such that H(m)=h), second preimage resistance (given m1, hard to find m2 with H(m1)=H(m2)), and collision resistance (hard to find any m1\u2260m2 with H(m1)=H(m2)). SHA-256 produces a 256-bit digest and is used in TLS, Bitcoin, and digital signatures. The avalanche effect \u2014 one input bit change should flip roughly 50% of output bits \u2014 is a key design criterion [6].

Key Exchange (Diffie-Hellman)

Published by Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman in 1976, the Diffie-Hellman protocol allows two parties to establish a shared secret over an insecure channel. Both pick private values, compute public values using modular exponentiation, exchange them, and derive the same shared secret independently. Security rests on the discrete logarithm problem: given g, p, and g^a mod p, finding a is believed computationally hard for large primes [7].

Key Parameters
PARAMETER	SYMBOL	TYPICAL VALUE	UNIT	DESCRIPTION
AES Key Length	k	128, 192, 256	bits	Determines number of rounds (10, 12, 14)
AES Block Size	b	128	bits	Fixed at 16 bytes for all AES variants
RSA Modulus Size	n	2048-4096	bits	Product of two primes; determines security level
RSA Public Exponent	e	65537	-	Commonly 2\u00b9\u2076+1 (Fermat prime F4)
SHA-256 Digest Length	-	256	bits	Fixed output regardless of input size
DH Prime Size	p	2048+	bits	Prime modulus for discrete log security
DH Generator	g	2 or 5	-	Primitive root modulo p
Caesar Key Space	-	26	keys	Trivially brute-forceable
Vigen\u00e8re Key Length	-	variable	chars	Longer keys improve security
Core Formulas
Caesar Cipher

Encryption: E(x) = (x + k) mod 26

Decryption: D(x) = (x - k) mod 26

Where x is the letter index (A=0, B=1, ..., Z=25) and k is the shift value.

RSA

Key Generation:

Choose primes p, q; compute n = p \u00d7 q
Compute \u03c6(n) = (p-1)(q-1)
Choose e such that gcd(e, \u03c6(n)) = 1
Compute d = e\u207b\u00b9 mod \u03c6(n)

Encryption: c = m^e mod n

Decryption: m = c^d mod n

Diffie-Hellman
Alice computes A = g^a mod p (sends A)
Bob computes B = g^b mod p (sends B)
Shared secret: s = B^a mod p = A^b mod p = g^(ab) mod p
AES MixColumns (GF(2\u2078))

Each column is multiplied by the fixed polynomial c(x) = 3x\u00b3 + x\u00b2 + x + 2 in GF(2\u2078) with irreducible polynomial m(x) = x\u2078 + x\u2074 + x\u00b3 + x + 1.

Avalanche Effect

Avalanche ratio = (number of differing output bits) / (total output bits)

Ideal target: 50% (each output bit has equal probability of flipping).

Learning Objectives

After completing this lab, you should be able to:

Encrypt and decrypt messages using Caesar and Vigen\u00e8re ciphers by hand
Trace AES-128 through all 10 rounds, identifying the purpose of each operation (SubBytes, ShiftRows, MixColumns, AddRoundKey)
Generate RSA key pairs from small primes and perform modular exponentiation
Demonstrate the avalanche effect by showing how single-bit input changes propagate through a hash function
Execute the Diffie-Hellman protocol and verify both parties arrive at the same shared secret
Analyze cipher weaknesses using frequency analysis on Caesar ciphertext and key-length detection on Vigen\u00e8re ciphertext
Compare symmetric vs. asymmetric encryption in terms of key distribution, performance, and use cases
Evaluate real-world protocol design by understanding why TLS uses hybrid encryption (asymmetric for key exchange, symmetric for data)
Historical Context and Evolution

The history of cryptography is essentially an arms race between code-makers and code-breakers. Understanding this history gives you perspective on why modern algorithms look the way they do.

Ancient Era (500 BC - 1800 AD): The Spartans used the scytale (a transposition cipher wrapping leather around a rod). Caesar\u2019s shift cipher appeared around 50 BC. The Arab mathematician Al-Kindi wrote the first known description of frequency analysis around 850 AD, which could break any monoalphabetic substitution cipher [3]. The Vigen\u00e8re cipher (1553) resisted frequency analysis for three centuries.

Mechanization (1900-1945): The Enigma machine used multiple rotors and a plugboard to create polyalphabetic substitution with a key space of approximately 1.59 \u00d7 10\u00b2\u2070 combinations. Alan Turing and the Bletchley Park team broke it by exploiting known-plaintext attacks (cribs) and the machine\u2019s constraint that no letter could encrypt to itself.

Modern Era (1970s-present): The publication of Diffie-Hellman (1976) and RSA (1977) revolutionized cryptography by separating encryption keys from decryption keys. DES (1977) standardized symmetric encryption, but its 56-bit key was broken by the EFF\u2019s "Deep Crack" machine in 1998. AES replaced DES in 2001 after a transparent, global competition. Today, post-quantum cryptography (lattice-based, hash-based) prepares for the eventual arrival of large-scale quantum computers.

In my experience, the pattern is always the same: someone invents a cipher they believe is unbreakable, and within a few decades (or centuries), someone else finds the mathematical structure that breaks it. The difference with AES and modern primitives is that they\u2019ve been designed with provable security margins \u2014 we know exactly how close the best attacks get, and that margin is enormous.

How This Simulation Works

This lab implements each cryptographic algorithm faithfully, with a few pedagogical simplifications:

Caesar and Vigen\u00e8re operate on the standard 26-letter Latin alphabet. The frequency analysis uses English letter frequencies from Lewand (2000).
AES-128 uses the complete FIPS 197 S-box and implements all four round operations (SubBytes, ShiftRows, MixColumns, AddRoundKey) with proper key expansion. The state grid displays column-major byte ordering as specified in the standard.
RSA uses small primes (< 1000) for visual clarity. The modular exponentiation uses square-and-multiply, the same algorithm used in production libraries (just with much larger numbers).
Hash visualization uses a simplified 128-bit hash function that demonstrates the avalanche effect. Real SHA-256 uses the Merkle-Damg\u00e5rd construction with 64 rounds per block, but the diffusion properties shown here are representative.
Diffie-Hellman uses small primes for interactivity. The color-mixing analogy makes the one-way nature of the discrete logarithm problem intuitive.
Exploration Activities
Activity 1: Breaking Caesar with Frequency Analysis
Enter a long English message (50+ characters) in the Caesar tab
Set shift to any value between 1-25
Observe the frequency analysis bars \u2014 the cipher frequency should look shifted relative to English
Try all 26 shifts and find which one makes the frequency bars align with the English reference
Note: the most common English letter is E (12.7%). Look for the highest cipher bar and calculate the shift
Record the brute force timing shown at the bottom \u2014 all 26 keys in under 1ms
Activity 2: AES Round-by-Round Walkthrough
Switch to the AES-128 tab
Enter a 16-character plaintext and key
Click "Next Step" to advance through each AES operation
Watch SubBytes change individual cells (non-linear substitution)
Watch ShiftRows rotate the rows by 0, 1, 2, and 3 positions
Watch MixColumns transform columns using GF(2\u2078) arithmetic
Compare the state after round 1 vs. round 10 \u2014 note how initial structure disappears
Activity 3: RSA with Deliberately Weak Primes
Switch to the RSA tab and set p=5, q=7
Note n=35 \u2014 this is trivially factorable
Encrypt a message and verify decryption works
Now try p=61, q=53 (n=3233) \u2014 still small but harder to factor mentally
Try p=2, q=3 and observe that RSA breaks (phi is too small)
Discuss: how does increasing prime size make factoring harder?
Activity 4: Diffie-Hellman Secret Agreement
Switch to the DH tab
Set p=23, g=5
Give Alice secret a=6, Bob secret b=15
Verify both sides compute the same shared secret
Now change Bob\u2019s secret to b=8 and verify the shared secret changes
Try imagining you\u2019re an eavesdropper: you see p=23, g=5, A=8, B=19 \u2014 can you find a or b?
Real-World Applications

TLS/HTTPS: Every secure web connection uses a combination of Diffie-Hellman (key exchange), AES (bulk encryption), and SHA-256 (message authentication). When you see the padlock icon, this is what runs underneath [8].

Cryptocurrency: Bitcoin uses SHA-256 for proof-of-work mining, ECDSA (elliptic curve variant of RSA-like signing) for transaction signatures, and Base58Check encoding which embeds hash checksums [6]. Understanding how SHA-256's avalanche properties work is also covered in depth in the Hash Collision Demonstrator, which visualizes birthday-paradox collision probability in real time.

Messaging apps: Signal Protocol (used by Signal, WhatsApp, Facebook Messenger) employs X3DH (Extended Triple Diffie-Hellman) for initial key agreement and AES-256 for message encryption.
